title.narrative: WHO AFRO COVID-19 implications on SRHR and mitigating risk of system collapse
WHO AFRO Covid-19 påverkan på SRHR och motverka risk för systemkollaps

description.narrative:
Konsekvenserna av covid-19 pandemin för låg- och medelinkomstländer riskerar bli katastrofala både vad gäller hälsoutfall och för den sociala och ekonomiska utvecklingen. I slutet av juni 2020 var antalet bekräftade fall av covid-19, som orsakas av coronavirus (SARS CoV-2), drygt 8,8 miljoner och 465 000 personer har avlidit. Afrika har än så länge relativt få fall, men WHO:s Regionkontor för Afrika (AFRO) uppskattar att 22 procent av befolkningen på den afrikanska kontinenten kommer att smittas under pandemins första år, vilket kan komma att resultera i 190 000 dödsfall. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) har nyligen publicerat en analys som visar att covid-19 Afrikas pandemi har haft samma utveckling under de första 150 dagarna som de kontinenter som drabbats tidigare.
Utöver direkta hälsokonsekvenserna av covid-19 visar ett antal prognoser att krishanteringen kan komma att tränga undan grundläggande hälso- och sjukvårdsinsatser, inklusive sexuell och reproduktiv hälsa och rättigheter (SRHR). Dessutom riskerar covid-19 responsen att finansiera punktinsatser istället för att beakta helhetsbehov och bygga motståndskraftiga system för att möjliggöra återhämtning. Erfarenhet från Ebola-epidemin visade att gravida kvinnors tillgång till mödrahälsovård minskade med förhöjd mödradödlighet som konsekvens. Tidiga uppgifter från covid-19 drabbade länder i regionen visar till exempel en ökning med 30% i antalet ärenden om könsrelaterat våld. Nyckelgrupper är särskilt sårbara på grund av minskat försörjning, stigma och diskriminering. Sida ser därmed en stor risk resultaten i Sveriges regionala SRHR strategi riskerar att påverkas negativt, vilket föranlett behovet av att stödja den kontinentala covid-19 responsen, med fokus på de indirekta effekterna av pandemin på SRHR.
Den 22 februari 2020 hölls ett krismöte med alla Afrikas 55 hälsoministrar/ hälsoministerier vilket resulterade i en kontinental strategi mot covid-19. Sydafrikas president, i egenskap av ordförande för Afrikanska Unionen, godkände strategin tillsammans med den byrå som bistår ordföranden, för närvarande presidenterna från Mali, Demokratiska Republiken Kongo, Egypten och Kenya. Den kontinentala covid-19 strategin Africa Joint Continental Strategy for COVID-19 Outbreak har två övergripande mål: 1) att förebygga svår sjukdom och död av coronavirusinfektion i medlemsländer och 2) att minimera sociala och ekonomiska konsekvenser av covid-19 utbrottet
Målsättningarna ska uppnås via två huvudsakliga arbetsspår: att samordna covid-19 responsen mellan medlemsländer, AU:s organ och WHO, och andra partners för att säkerställa synergier och att minska risker för dubbelarbete samt genom att främja evidensbaserade folkhälsostrategier för övervakning (surveillance), förebyggande arbete, diagnos, behandling och kontroll av covid-19.
Strategin implementeras genom Africa Task Force for Coronavirus (AFTCOR), där Africa CDC, FN och AU:s medlemsländer leder arbetsgrupper, och genom Africa CDC’s Incident Management System (IMS). Ett antal partners, både FN och ickestatliga aktörer, bidrar också till att implementera strategin. Dessa implementerande partners finansieras antingen direkt av biståndsgivare som finansierar kompletterande insatser, eller via Africa CDC som sedan vidareförmedlar medel till implementerande partners. Ett tillägg finns även till strategin, AU COVID-19 Pandemic Preparedness and Response Plan Addendum to the African Union COVID-19- Continental Strategy, som inkluderar specifik referens till att säkerställa tillgång till grundläggande hälsosjukvård, inklusive mödrabarnhälsovård under covid-19 pandemin.
Sida kommer att bidra till Africa Joint Continental Strategy for COVID-19 Outbreak genom två nya insatser och en avtalsändring av en pågående insats, 2Gether4SRHR (insats ID: 10596, beslutsnummer ZAM-DC19/2020). De två nya insatserna är till Africa CDC om SEK 20 000 000 och till WHO AFRO om SEK 30 000 000. Sida ser på insatserna som tre delar av ett sammanhållet stöd i linje med ovan nämnda strategi, dvs Africa Joint Continental Strategy for COVID-19 Outbreak.
WHO AFRO har sökt om finansiering för programmet Country Level AFRO Reform (DCL): From COVID to HEALTH (2020–2021), som är uppdelat på två pelare. Pelare ett: COVID-19 implications on essential health service delivery (i.e., SRHR) and mitigating the risk of system collapse och pelare två: Coordinated Strategic and Policy Support for Structural and Functional Transformation of WHO Country Offices under perioden 1 juli 2020 till 31 december 2021. Sida kommer att finanserna pelare ett med 30 miljoner SEK och UD finansiera pelare två med 50 Miljoner SEK (Beslut UD2020/08919/IU, UD2020/01985/FN). Den totala volymen är 80 miljoner SEK. Insatsen finansieras via en s.k. pooled fund som administreras av WHO AFRO, som är avtalspart. Aktiviteterna under pelare ett kommer att genomföras inom WHO AFRO regionen, med följande fokusländer: Sierra Leone, Kenya, Burkina Faso, Kamerun, Nigeria, Centralafrikanska Republiken och Demokratiska Republiken Kongo och genom stärkt kapacitet för samordning på det WHO:s regionala kontor för AFRO-regionen i Brazzaville.

WHO AFRO has applied to Sweden for funding of 80 million SEK to carry out the " Country Level AFRO Reform (DCL): From COVID to HEALTH), which is divided into two pillars. Pillar 1: COVID-19 implications on essential health service delivery (i.e., SRHR) and mitigating the risk of system collapse" and pillar two “Coordinated Strategic and Policy Support for Structural and Functional Transformation of WHO Country Offices.” The programme will be implemented between 1 July 2020 and 31 December 2021. Sida will contribute 30 Million SEK to pillar one and the Ministry for Foreign Affairs (MFA) will contribute 50 million SEK to pillar two.
The funding will be used to strengthen and amplify the convening power, influence, and mandate of the WHO/AFRO to offer quality and timely technical support to the focus countries. More specifically, this Grant will allow WHO/AFRO to support the focus countries in achieving the following outcomes:
1. Maintained continuity of essential high-quality SRHR information and services through a health system approach, including preventing and responding to sexual and gender-based violence 2. Increased access to a wider range of contraceptive methods (expanded method mix) through Task Sharing and self-care interventions 3. Strengthened monitoring system for tracking progress in SRHR/Family Planning.
This investment will enable WHO-AFRO to contribute to components of its Transformation Agenda 2015-2020—pro-results values, smart technical focus; responsive strategic operations; and effective communication and partnerships in the SRHR workspace. It will also contribute to the Regional WHO transformation aiming at understanding the country’s priorities as well as the type and level of support required and align WHO country presence to the Member States and partner expectations (linked to Pillar II).
WHO AFRO will implement the contribution in close coronation with 2Gether4SRHR (ID: 10596), in particular the agreement amended (ZAM-DC19/2020). The total budget of the contribution is 80 Million SEK, where Sida contributes 30 MSEK and the Swedish Ministry for Foreign Affairs 50 MSEK (Decision UD2020/08919/IU, UD2020/01985/FN) .
The contribution is in line with the Africa Joint Continental Strategy for COVID-19 Outbreak.

The objectives of the intervention have not been changed. This intervention supports the WHO AFRO implementation of the Country Level AFRO Reform (DCL): From COVID to HEALTH, "Pillar 1: COVID-19 implications on essential health service delivery (i.e., SRHR) and mitigating the risk of system collapse". The initiative will strengthen and amplify the convening power, influence, and mandate of the WHO AFRO to offer quality and timely technical support to focus countries, in order to achieve the following outcomes: 1. Maintained continuity of essential high-quality SRHR information and services through a health system approach, including preventing and responding to sexual and gender-based violence 2. Increased access to a wider range of contraceptive methods (expanded method mix) through Task Sharing and self-care interventions 3. Strengthened monitoring system for tracking progress in SRHR/Family Planning. Additional funding to Pillar 2 “Coordinated Strategic and Policy Support for Structural and Functional Transformation of WHO Country Offices” is channeled trough the Swedish Ministry for Foreign Affairs.

sector.narrative: Basic Health Care Services in Emergencies
Ending violence against women and girls

description.narrative:
Over the four-year period between 2020 and 2024, the WHO in the African Region (WHO/AFRO) delivered technical and financial support interventions across 17 countries primarily in the West and Central Africa sub-region. The project titled "Pillar 1 Grant on COVID-19 implications on essential health service delivery and mitigating the risk of system collapse", has been funded by Sida's regional strategy for SRHR in Africa 2022-2026. The aim was to maintain sexual and reproductive health services and reduce maternal mortality during the COVID-19 pandemic and beyond in the post-pandemic recovery phase. As COVID-19 spread worldwide, it quickly became clear that the response to the pandemic severely restricted access to SRHR services. Factors such as disrupted supply chains, national stay-at-home orders, and treatment protocols made it difficult for women to receive essential health care. This disruption heavily impacted health services, reducing the availability of SRHR services, such as family planning counselling and contraception provision, abortion care, maternal and child health services, and services related to HIV/AIDS and sexually transmitted infections, along with support for survivors of gender-based violence. Routine essential SRHR services were de-prioritized in some countries, potentially worsening inequities due to societal responses to the pandemic. These responses included reallocating resources to control COVID-19, lock-downs that forced the closure of non-prioritized health services, disrupted supplies, and the effects of physical distancing, travel restrictions, and economic slowdowns.
The project contributed to maintaining sexual and reproductive health services by building the commitment, skills and capacity of national officials, service providers, and local community partners in SRHR services with a clear health system strengthening approach. The working model was to cooperate with ministries of health, professional associations, WHO country offices, and local community-based organizations to support SRHR interventions; to disseminate WHO guidelines and latest evidence-based recommendations on SRHR and provide high-quality training to policy makers, managers and frontline healthcare workers.
Key SRHR services targeted in the project were family planning and contraceptive services, abortion care, maternal health, SGBV and comprehensive sexuality education, CSE. WHO innovations such as self-care for SRHR helped drive change and positive project results during the COVID-19 lockdown. The project has shown that with adequate training, supply of essential commodities and supervision, self-care interventions can support formal efforts to improve maternal health outcomes in supported countries.
Given the broad scope and coverage of this WHO-led SRHR project, several results were achieved over the project period. First and foremost, it is necessary to highlight that the general assumption that maternal mortality rates would drastically increase during and after the pandemic, did not materialize. In fact, the pre-pandemic trend with declining maternal mortality rates was maintained during the COVID-19 pandemic period. While there was a notable rise in maternal mortality rates in 12 out of these 17 countries during 2021 due to COVID-19, most nations bounced back, showing a decline in the following years. Among those countries, the most significant increases in maternal mortality deaths from 2020 to 2021 were observed in Kenya (up 3.7% from 489 to 507), the Republic of Congo (up 21.9% from 247 to 301), and Gabon (up 28.5% from 194 to 249). However, some countries managed to achieve reductions during this time, including Sierra Leone (from 422 to 403) and the Central African Republic (from 1296 to 1127). The overall downward trend in maternal mortality, even among countries that experienced slight increases early in the pandemic, underscores the resilience and effectiveness of their healthcare systems.
Notable over-arching results on outcome level to which the project contributed, include:
1) Women of reproductive age who received modern contraceptive methods increased by 45% The number of reproductive-age women using modern contraceptives grew by 45%, from 8.4 million in 2019 to 12.3 million in 2023. Fifteen countries tracked and reported this data.
2) 85% increase in women receiving abortion care services The 85% increase refers to women who received post abortion services from a baseline of 270,000 in 2019 to 500,000 in 2023. 11 countries monitored and reported on this indicator.
3) Births attended by skilled health personnel increased by over 60% The number of births attended by skilled health personnel rose by more than 60%, increasing from 14 million in 2019 to 22.5 million in 2023. Fifteen countries tracked and reported this indicator. While Burundi and Gabon showed a decrease in health facility deliveries, a recovery and consistent increase followed in the years that followed.
4) Sexual and Gender-Based Violence survivors who received care rose nearly fourfold The number of SGBV survivors receiving care surged nearly fourfold, rising from 30,000 in 2019 to 117,000 in 2023. Across all 14 countries that tracked this indicator, a significant rise in SGBV survivors accessing care was noted. For instance, in Nigeria, the figures increased from 4,777 in 2020 to 48,055 in 2023.
Selected results from particular countries (specific data are found in the final report) include:
1) Despite challenges such as delays in fund release and coordination issues, the program successfully integrated SRHR services with family planning, HIV counselling, and cervical cancer screening in Sierra Leone. Community engagement and campaigns were pivotal in raising awareness and reducing cultural barriers to family planning. Overall, the program contributed to improving maternal health outcomes, increased skilled deliveries, and better access to SRHR services, demonstrating its critical role in advancing public health.
2) In the Republic of Congo, training guides for family planning providers and monitoring labour were created. The RMNCAH Integrated Strategy 2022-2026 was implemented, significantly improving access to SRHR services. Training was provided to 90% of health centre and hospital providers in the 12 target districts, leading to increased use of SRHR services and a notable decrease in maternal deaths, from 473 per 100,000 live births in 2020 to 304 per 100,000 in 2023. The average rate of skilled birth attendance also rose from 9% in 2020 to 28% in 2022 in targeted areas.
3) In Togo, teachers were trained to raise awareness among students, and a code of conduct was developed to guide teachings, particularly to reduce unsafe abortions among girls. The integration of drug consumption themes led to fewer complaints about illicit drug use. School clubs were established to train students to raise awareness among their peers, and efforts to promote vaccination were successful. A law was drafted to abolish the exclusion of pregnant young girls from school. Health providers received training to strengthen their capacities, with 500 providers trained in 2024.
4) In Guinea, strengthening the surveillance of maternal and perinatal deaths and response through training of review committees, monitoring their operations and quarterly reviews of response plans have had a significant impact according to the evaluation of the project.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
